item.title: What Chinese President Xi Jinping’s Five BRICS Proposals Mean for the Next Phase of Cooperation
item.dc:creator: Mesafint Brlie
item.description: Addis Ababa, September 18, 2026 (FMC) — Five-point plans put forward by Chinese President Xi Jinping at the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi last week offer a broad picture of where practical cooperation among the expanded grouping could head next, placing artificial intelligence, trade, digital industries, smart manufacturing and technological talent at the center […]
item.content:encoded:
Addis Ababa, September 18, 2026 (FMC) — Five-point plans put forward by Chinese President Xi Jinping at the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi last week offer a broad picture of where practical cooperation among the expanded grouping could head next, placing artificial intelligence, trade, digital industries, smart manufacturing and technological talent at the center of its emerging agenda.

The proposals were not presented as isolated initiatives. Taken together, they point to an effort to connect technology, production, skills and markets in ways that could strengthen the economic foundations of BRICS cooperation and create new avenues for collaboration among member countries and the wider Global South.

At a media briefing in Addis Ababa on Thursday, Chinese Embassy Chargé d’Affaires a.i. Sun Mingxi returned to the proposals while explaining China’s priorities following the New Delhi summit. His briefing offered a closer look at the areas China sees as particularly important for advancing practical cooperation under BRICS.

The first proposal — an open-source and inclusive artificial intelligence initiative — addresses one of the defining technological questions of the coming years.

China proposed establishing a BRICS AI open-source community, supporting cooperation in the development and application of large language models, and organizing specialized AI seminars and training courses. The broader objective is to build an open AI ecosystem through cooperation among BRICS countries.

The proposal is significant because artificial intelligence is rapidly moving from a specialized technology into an important component of economic production, public services, scientific research and industrial competitiveness.

For developing economies, participation in this transformation is increasingly about more than acquiring finished technologies. It involves developing skills, research capacity, computing capabilities and locally relevant applications, while ensuring that new technologies can respond to different languages, cultures and development circumstances.

This makes the open-source dimension particularly relevant to countries seeking to expand their own technological capabilities.

Cooperation in large language models, research and training could create channels through which BRICS members contribute to and benefit from a broader technological ecosystem.

The second proposal moves from technology to the economic environment in which technology and production can generate value: trade and investment facilitation.

China proposed establishing a BRICS special economic zone partnership, including an intelligent portal for policy coordination and open economic cooperation. It also proposed holding a BRICS Forum on Trade in Services in 2027 to develop new drivers of economic and trade cooperation.

The significance of this proposal extends beyond conventional trade in goods.

Services, digital commerce, investment and technology-enabled business are becoming increasingly important components of international economic relations.

Greater coordination among BRICS economies could therefore help connect businesses and investors across markets while making it easier to navigate different regulatory and policy environments.

For economies such as Ethiopia that are seeking greater integration into international markets, this dimension of BRICS cooperation is particularly relevant.

The third proposal focuses directly on the digital economy.

China proposed establishing a BRICS digital ecosystem cloud platform and expanding digital-skills training, technological exchanges and industrial alignment to jointly advance digital economic development.

This proposal suggests a shift from viewing digital transformation primarily through the lens of connectivity toward building an ecosystem in which digital infrastructure, skills, technology and industry reinforce one another.

That distinction is increasingly important.

A country may have widespread access to digital services without necessarily possessing the capacity to develop digital products, operate advanced platforms or create technology-intensive industries. Digital skills and technological exchange can therefore become as important as the infrastructure itself.

For Ethiopia, which is expanding digital public infrastructure, digital identification, electronic payments and digital skills while placing artificial intelligence increasingly within its development agenda, this area of the proposed BRICS cooperation has obvious points of intersection.

The fourth proposal addresses the productive side of the equation: intelligent manufacturing.

China has proposed supporting BRICS countries in building smart factories, developing standards and norms, and jointly advancing manufacturing transformation and upgrading.

The proposal comes at a time when manufacturing is being reshaped by artificial intelligence, automation, robotics, data analytics and interconnected production systems.

For countries pursuing industrialization, the question is increasingly not simply how to expand manufacturing capacity, but how to make that capacity more productive, technologically capable and competitive.

Smart manufacturing can potentially help bridge that gap by bringing advanced technologies into factories and production chains while creating opportunities for technical cooperation and skills development.

This has particular relevance for African economies seeking to increase domestic value addition. The transition from exporting raw materials toward processing, manufacturing and higher-value production requires not only investment but also technology, technical expertise and access to markets.

The fifth proposal addresses the human foundation required to make the other four possible.

China proposed establishing a BRICS engineer cultivation alliance for joint development of engineers and mutual recognition of competency standards. It also announced a BRICS youth exchange program focused on scientific and technological innovation.

The emphasis on talent is important because technology transfer and industrial upgrading ultimately depend on people capable of developing, operating, adapting and improving the technologies involved.

Engineers, researchers, programmers, technicians and other skilled professionals form the human infrastructure of the digital and industrial economies.

The five proposals therefore form a connected chain.

AI requires talent and digital infrastructure. Digital industries require skills and technological exchange. Smart manufacturing requires engineers, investment and technology. Trade facilitation provides pathways for the resulting goods and services to reach wider markets.

Seen together, the proposals point toward a model of BRICS cooperation in which technology, industrial development, human capital and trade are increasingly treated as interconnected components of economic transformation.

That broader approach also explains why the proposals were placed within Xi Jinping’s call for BRICS countries to strengthen their economic foundations, safeguard stable industrial and supply chains, foster a large integrated market, build innovation incubators, upgrade traditional industries and develop emerging and future industries.

The proposals also need to be viewed against China’s own development trajectory.

Xi said China’s 15th Five-Year Plan, launched this year, represents not only a blueprint for China’s economic and social development but also a “cooperation list” for the rest of the world. He linked the plan to high-quality development, high-standard opening up, the Global Development Initiative and high-quality Belt and Road cooperation.

This places the five BRICS proposals within a broader Chinese emphasis on technological advancement, industrial upgrading and international economic cooperation.

The message is that China’s own development experience and capabilities can increasingly be connected with opportunities in partner economies, while cooperation with those economies can also create new markets, production links and avenues for shared development.

For BRICS, that approach could become particularly significant as the grouping seeks to translate its growing economic weight into more practical cooperation.

The expanded BRICS brings together economies with different levels of development, industrial structures, technological capabilities and resource bases. The challenge is therefore not simply to identify common interests, but to build mechanisms through which those interests can generate concrete cooperation.

The five proposals offer several such mechanisms: an AI community, a special economic zone partnership, a digital ecosystem platform, cooperation on smart factories and standards, and joint development of technical talent.

Their potential significance for Ethiopia is also clear.

Ethiopia is pursuing digital transformation and artificial intelligence while seeking to expand manufacturing, strengthen domestic production, increase value addition and deepen access to international markets. Its BRICS engagement has likewise emphasized opportunities in technology, agriculture, minerals, renewable energy and industrial development.

The overlap means that cooperation in AI, digital skills, industrial technology, manufacturing and trade services could potentially complement Ethiopia’s own development priorities.

But the importance of the proposals extends beyond any individual BRICS member.

For Africa and other developing regions, the central question is whether cooperation among emerging economies can contribute to building productive capabilities — whether in technology, manufacturing, skills, agriculture, energy or services — rather than simply expanding the exchange of finished products.

This is where the proposals on talent and technology become especially important.

Access to advanced technology without the skills to adapt it can create dependence. Investment without domestic productive capacity may have limited transformational impact. Market access without competitive production may not generate sustained export growth.

The five proposals, taken together, address several of these dimensions at once.

Their eventual impact, however, will depend on implementation: whether proposed platforms become functioning mechanisms, whether training produces usable skills, whether technological exchanges generate domestic capacity, whether smart-manufacturing cooperation reaches actual production systems, and whether trade facilitation creates new opportunities for businesses.

That implementation phase is now the more important question following the New Delhi summit.

The proposals have already moved the discussion beyond broad statements about cooperation toward identifiable areas in which BRICS countries can build institutions, platforms, skills and industrial partnerships.

For China, they also provide a framework for advancing its priorities in technology, industry, trade and human-capital development through the BRICS mechanism.

For the wider grouping, they offer potential pathways for turning the economic weight and diversity of BRICS into practical cooperation.

And for countries such as Ethiopia, the significance lies in the possibility of connecting national development ambitions with a broader network of technology, investment, markets and skills.

The next phase will therefore be measured less by the announcement of the five proposals than by what follows from them — the partnerships they generate, the capabilities they build and the extent to which they contribute to a more productive, technologically capable and interconnected BRICS community.

item.title: Why Ethiopia Emerged as the Champion of the New Delhi BRICS Summit
item.dc:creator: Mesafint Brlie
item.description: Addis Ababa, September 18, 2026 (FMC) — Ethiopia arrived at the 18th BRICS Leaders’ Summit in New Delhi as a relatively new member of the grouping. It left with its economic transformation, strategic priorities and broader international ambitions firmly placed within the discussions of some of the world’s major emerging economies. That performance prompted Chinese […]
item.content:encoded:
Addis Ababa, September 18, 2026 (FMC) — Ethiopia arrived at the 18th BRICS Leaders’ Summit in New Delhi as a relatively new member of the grouping.

It left with its economic transformation, strategic priorities and broader international ambitions firmly placed within the discussions of some of the world’s major emerging economies.

That performance prompted Chinese Embassy Chargé d’Affaires a.i. Sun Mingxi, speaking to the media in Addis Ababa on Thursday, to describe Ethiopia as the “champion” of the recent BRICS Summit.

The characterization is striking not simply because of the diplomatic endorsements Ethiopia received, but because of the breadth of what the country brought to the summit and the extent to which its national priorities intersected with the issues at the heart of the BRICS agenda.

Ethiopia’s participation in New Delhi was therefore about more than securing support for individual candidacies.

It was an opportunity to present a country undergoing economic and technological transformation, seeking deeper integration into global markets, advancing its productive capacity and positioning itself as an active contributor to the evolving architecture of the Global South.

At the center of that presentation was a changing Ethiopian economy.

Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed used the summit to highlight Ethiopia’s progress in food security, particularly the country’s movement from dependence on imported wheat toward domestic production and self-sufficiency.

The shift carries significance beyond agriculture: it reflects a wider effort to expand productive capacity, reduce import dependence and turn Ethiopia from a consumer of strategic commodities into an increasingly important producer and potential supplier.

The Prime Minister linked that transformation to the idea of a BRICS grain exchange, placing Ethiopia’s agricultural progress within a broader conversation about food security, trade and cooperation among emerging economies.

That same logic extends to other areas of domestic production.

Ethiopia’s push to expand pharmaceutical manufacturing and local value creation points to an economy seeking not merely to import finished goods, but to develop the capacity to produce, process and supply more of what it consumes and, increasingly, what regional and international markets require.

Digital transformation provided another important part of Ethiopia’s presentation.

The country has been building digital public infrastructure around digital identification, electronic payments and secure data exchange, while placing artificial intelligence increasingly at the center of its development agenda.

In New Delhi, Ethiopia argued that Africa should not remain merely a market for technologies developed elsewhere, but should participate in shaping artificial intelligence around its own languages, knowledge systems, communities and development needs.

That message fitted naturally into a BRICS agenda increasingly concerned with artificial intelligence, digital transformation, technological cooperation and the question of how developing economies can acquire the capabilities needed to participate in the next phase of global economic change.

Ethiopia also brought its renewable-energy potential, green-development experience and climate agenda into the summit conversation.

Its Green Legacy Initiative, expanding renewable-energy base and broader efforts around climate-resilient development provide the country with an economic and environmental proposition at a time when BRICS cooperation is increasingly addressing energy, climate finance, sustainable development and technology.

The country’s preparations to host and preside over COP32 in 2027 added an important international dimension to that agenda. The New Delhi Declaration expressed support for Ethiopia’s COP32 presidency, placing the country’s climate diplomacy within the collective BRICS framework.

Ethiopia’s resource base and industrial ambitions also fit into the wider BRICS discussion on industrialization, value addition and access to technology, capital and markets.

The country is seeking to move beyond the traditional export of raw materials by developing processing and manufacturing capacity, while using its membership in BRICS to connect domestic opportunities with larger pools of investment, technology and demand.

Connectivity was another defining thread.

Ethiopia’s aviation network, centered on Ethiopian Airlines, gives the country a distinctive position in African and international connectivity. Addis Ababa’s role as the headquarters of the African Union further reinforces its position as a diplomatic and institutional center on the continent.

But physical connectivity for Ethiopia extends beyond aviation.

Its expanding logistics infrastructure, including the recently expanded Modjo Dry Port, reflects the country’s effort to strengthen its position along regional trade corridors and reduce the costs and delays associated with moving goods.

At the broader BRICS level, discussions on trade facilitation, payments, logistics, investment and economic connectivity create a framework in which such national infrastructure ambitions can connect with wider regional and global markets.

This is also where Ethiopia’s longstanding pursuit of reliable access to the sea takes on a wider economic meaning.

At New Delhi, the issue was framed not simply as a geographical question but as an economic imperative linked to trade, market access, connectivity and the cost of doing business.

For one of Africa’s largest landlocked economies, reliable and diversified access to international trade routes is closely connected to its ambitions to expand production, attract investment and deepen commercial relations with BRICS economies and the wider world.

Ethiopia has continued to emphasize that this objective should be pursued through peaceful and negotiated arrangements.

Seen in this wider context, Ethiopia’s BRICS strategy was not simply about asking what the grouping could do for Ethiopia.

It was increasingly about demonstrating what Ethiopia itself could bring to the partnership: agricultural production, a large and growing market, renewable-energy potential, critical resources, aviation connectivity, digital capabilities and an expanding productive base.

That distinction matters.

BRICS brings together major markets, financial institutions, technological capabilities, energy producers and increasingly influential economies of the Global South.

Ethiopia’s proposition is that its own transformation can complement those strengths through investment, trade, technology transfer, industrial cooperation and stronger physical and digital connectivity.

The New Delhi Summit also gave Ethiopia concrete diplomatic dividends.

BRICS members expressed strong support for Ethiopia’s accession to the World Trade Organization, welcomed its candidacy for an additional seat on the International Civil Aviation Organization Council — where Ethiopia is the sole African candidate endorsed by the African Union for the additional seat — and expressed support for Ethiopia’s presidency of COP32.

These outcomes matter in different ways.

Support for Ethiopia’s WTO accession aligns with the country’s ambition to deepen its integration into the multilateral trading system.

Backing for its ICAO candidacy recognizes Ethiopia’s longstanding role in African and international aviation. Support for COP32, meanwhile, strengthens Ethiopia’s position as Africa prepares to host another major global climate process.

Together, they connect Ethiopia’s domestic economic transformation with three wider international arenas: global trade, international aviation governance and climate diplomacy.

The summit therefore offered Ethiopia something broader than individual endorsements.

It provided a platform from which the country could connect its domestic development agenda to the major questions confronting emerging economies — food security, industrialization, digital transformation, energy transition, climate resilience, trade, connectivity and reform of global institutions.

That broader positioning is particularly significant for a country that joined BRICS only in 2024.

In a relatively short period, Ethiopia has moved from being a new entrant to using the platform to articulate both national and African priorities.

Its interventions in New Delhi included calls for stronger BRICS-Africa cooperation, greater value creation and economic resilience, alongside proposals and positions addressing technology, food security, climate action and global governance.

The New Delhi Declaration itself reflects many of these intersections.

It contains provisions on WTO reform, agriculture, digital agriculture, industrial and technological cooperation, AI, climate action and greater representation of developing countries in global institutions.

Its support for Ethiopia’s WTO, ICAO and COP32 priorities therefore came within a much broader agenda that closely overlaps with Ethiopia’s own development and diplomatic priorities.

There was consequently a two-way calculation in New Delhi.

Ethiopia was seeking markets, investment, technology, connectivity and greater space in global institutions.

At the same time, its growing economy, strategic location, agricultural potential, renewable resources, aviation network and large domestic market offered areas in which BRICS cooperation could generate practical value.

That is what gives the “champion” description its wider context.

It was not simply about how many formal references Ethiopia secured in a declaration.

It was about how extensively the country’s development trajectory, economic interests and international ambitions intersected with the priorities being debated by the BRICS economies — and how effectively Ethiopia used its place at the table to turn those intersections into diplomatic and economic opportunities.

For Ethiopia, New Delhi was therefore less a single summit moment than a convergence point: domestic transformation meeting global economic ambition, African priorities meeting the expanding BRICS agenda, and national development goals being translated into a broader international proposition.

The immediate endorsements are now part of the record.

The larger significance will depend on what Ethiopia does with the space that New Delhi opened — turning diplomatic backing into trade opportunities, investment, technology partnerships, stronger connectivity, institutional influence and tangible economic gains.

That is ultimately where the importance of Ethiopia’s BRICS moment lies: not simply in being recognized at the summit, but in using recognition to advance the transformation already underway at home and to build stronger links between Ethiopia, Africa and the wider emerging global economy.

item.title: Ethiopia Puts Knowledge, Digital Services and Local Capacity at Center of New Africa-Europe Partnerships
item.dc:creator: Mesafint Brlie
item.description: Addis Ababa, September 18, 2026 (FMC) — Ethiopia has highlighted the growing importance of services trade in advancing structural transformation, economic diversification, employment and sustainable development in Africa at the World Trade Organization (WTO) Public Forum 2026 in Geneva. The emphasis came during a session titled “Services Trade for Development Partnerships: Italy and Africa,” organized […]
item.content:encoded:
Addis Ababa, September 18, 2026 (FMC) — Ethiopia has highlighted the growing importance of services trade in advancing structural transformation, economic diversification, employment and sustainable development in Africa at the World Trade Organization (WTO) Public Forum 2026 in Geneva.

The emphasis came during a session titled “Services Trade for Development Partnerships: Italy and Africa,” organized by the Permanent Mission of Italy and co-organized with the United Nations Trade and Development (UNCTAD) and the International Trade Centre (ITC).

Ambassador Negus Kebede, Minister Plenipotentiary on WTO Affairs at the Permanent Mission of Ethiopia in Geneva, participated as a panelist, stressing that effective services partnerships should create lasting value through knowledge transfer, technology, skills development and local capacity-building.

He highlighted the role of services across agriculture, manufacturing and infrastructure, as well as the growing importance of digital and knowledge-intensive services in Africa’s economic transformation.

Ambassador Negus also highlighted Ethiopia’s cooperation with Italy in major infrastructure and hydropower projects, citing the contributions of Italian companies including Salini Costruttori, now part of Webuild, and Studio Pietrangeli.

He stressed the importance of combining international expertise with African ownership, local capabilities and long-term development priorities.

Highlighting Ethiopia’s own experience, he cited Digital Ethiopia 2030 and Ethiopian Airlines as examples of efforts to build competitive capabilities in digital and knowledge-intensive services, logistics, aviation, training and related sectors.

Ambassador Negus said Africa should move beyond being a market for digital technologies and develop the capacity to become a producer and exporter of digital and knowledge-intensive services.

He called for a new generation of partnerships based on co-investment, co-production, co-innovation and shared value creation, emphasizing that successful partnerships should go beyond delivering projects to building the capacity needed to develop the next generation of services and enterprises.

Ethiopia’s participation reflects its continued engagement in the WTO Public Forum 2026, which brings together governments, international organizations, businesses, civil society and academia to discuss emerging issues shaping the multilateral trading system and global trade.

item.title: Ethiopia Enters New Year With Focus on Delivery, National Dialogue and Mega Development Projects: GCS
item.dc:creator: Mesafint Brlie
item.description: Addis Ababa, September 18, 2026 (FMC) — Ethiopia’s new year marks more than a change in the calendar, with the country opening what the FDRE Government Communication Service (GCS) described as a new chapter shaped by national choices, consultation, resilience and development. In a message shared Friday, the GCS said Ethiopia has recorded achievements over […]
item.content:encoded:
Addis Ababa, September 18, 2026 (FMC) — Ethiopia’s new year marks more than a change in the calendar, with the country opening what the FDRE Government Communication Service (GCS) described as a new chapter shaped by national choices, consultation, resilience and development.

In a message shared Friday, the GCS said Ethiopia has recorded achievements over the past few years that had remained unattained for decades, attributing the progress to sustained efforts and a new culture of setting ambitious goals, starting projects and completing them.

The message highlighted the national dialogue process, saying Ethiopians from across the country have gathered to deliberate on the future of their country, reflect on national issues and freely present ideas they believe can contribute to the national interest.

It also pointed to government measures involving pardons and the release of political prisoners, describing them as steps taken alongside efforts to uphold the rule of law and promote reconciliation. The GCS said such measures are intended to help break cycles of retaliation and strengthen national consensus.

The message linked political and social stability with economic progress and public confidence, highlighting what it described as Ethiopia’s strong economic performance and the expansion of its productive capacity.

It cited the expansion of wheat production, particularly summer wheat, as evidence of Ethiopia’s progress toward greater self-reliance in food production. The GCS also highlighted the country’s large-scale tree-planting campaigns, saying Ethiopia has repeatedly surpassed its previous records and emerged as an example of international environmental cooperation.

The message further highlighted developments in renewable energy, mineral resources, tourism, conference tourism and urban development. It said new tourism destinations are being developed while Ethiopia’s existing cultural and historical heritage is being rehabilitated and preserved for future generations.

Digital transformation was also identified as a major area of focus, with the GCS saying Ethiopia is implementing the Digital Ethiopia 2030 strategy and laying the foundations for a more transparent and efficient government administration.

On foreign policy, the message said Ethiopia has strengthened its focus on national interests and has sought to assert the country’s interests more firmly on the international stage.

The GCS also highlighted institution building, saying efforts have been made to strengthen institutions in the justice, security and democratic sectors. It said the country is developing institutional capacity designed to support long-term national development and withstand changes in political systems.

The message emphasized the government’s stated approach of starting projects and seeing them through to completion. It cited the reopening of previously closed industries, the transition of loss-making institutions toward profitability, and progress in investment, exports and import-substituting production.

Looking ahead, the GCS highlighted major projects announced following the completion of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), saying projects valued at more than 30 billion U.S. dollars have been announced in Guba as part of Ethiopia’s future development plans.

Among the projects highlighted is a nuclear facility, for which the GCS said a new agreement has been signed and work has begun as part of efforts to strengthen energy security. It also pointed to the development of Ethiopia’s natural-gas resources and gas-processing projects in the Somali Regional State.

The planned Bishoftu International Airport was highlighted as another major undertaking. The GCS said the airport is designed to accommodate 100 million passengers annually and will strengthen Ethiopia’s aviation capacity.

A fertilizer manufacturing project expected to save Ethiopia more than 1 billion U.S. dollars annually was also cited, with the GCS saying it is expected to support agricultural productivity and ease pressure on farmers.

The message further said work has begun, in cooperation with international institutions, on a program to develop 1.5 million homes, an initiative the GCS said will have a significant impact on the lives of many people.

The GCS said Ethiopia’s development journey will continue with consultation and collective effort, stressing that there remains substantial work ahead and that the country will continue pursuing its aspirations through both deliberation and implementation.

It concluded by underscoring the principle of turning commitments into completed action and fulfilling promises as part of the foundations being laid for future generations.

item.title: Ethiopia Showcases Citizen-Centered Digital Government Model at HUAWEI Connect 2026 in Shanghai
item.dc:creator: Mesafint Brlie
item.description: Addis Ababa, September 18, 2026 (FMC) — Ethiopia’s MESOB Service has presented the country’s experience and lessons in digital government service delivery at HUAWEI Connect 2026 in Shanghai, China. The presentation showcased MESOB’s emerging digital government service ecosystem and Ethiopia’s efforts to advance citizen-centered, integrated and accessible public services. The international technology event provided a […]
item.content:encoded:
Addis Ababa, September 18, 2026 (FMC) — Ethiopia’s MESOB Service has presented the country’s experience and lessons in digital government service delivery at HUAWEI Connect 2026 in Shanghai, China.

The presentation showcased MESOB’s emerging digital government service ecosystem and Ethiopia’s efforts to advance citizen-centered, integrated and accessible public services.

The international technology event provided a platform for Ethiopia to share its experience in developing a digital government service ecosystem and lessons from its ongoing efforts to make public services more integrated and accessible.

MESOB’s participation highlighted Ethiopia’s drive to place citizens at the center of digital public service delivery through an integrated approach to government services.

HUAWEI CONNECT 2026, running from September 17 to 19 in Shanghai, is bringing together technology and industry stakeholders to explore advances in artificial intelligence, digital transformation and intelligent infrastructure.

The event is being held at the Shanghai World Expo Exhibition & Convention Center and Shanghai Expo Center under the theme “Advancing the Agentic World.”

item.title: 300 militants of the illegal TPLF group surrender to ENDF, hand over more than 280 weapons
item.dc:creator: Mesafint Brlie
item.description: Addis Ababa, September 18, 2026 (FMC) — Nearly 300 militants of the illegal TPLF have surrendered to the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) Northwestern Command in the Tekeze area, handing over more than 280 individual and group weapons, large quantities of ammunition, battlefield optical equipment and various documents. The combatants surrendered in the Tekeze direction […]
item.content:encoded:
Addis Ababa, September 18, 2026 (FMC) — Nearly 300 militants of the illegal TPLF have surrendered to the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) Northwestern Command in the Tekeze area, handing over more than 280 individual and group weapons, large quantities of ammunition, battlefield optical equipment and various documents.

The combatants surrendered in the Tekeze direction of the western front, on both sides of the Tekeze Bridge, ENDF online media team told Fana Media Corporation.

The militants said they chose not to continue fighting for the banned TPLF in opposition to its preparations for war, and surrendered after establishing contact with the ENDF in the area, holding discussions and arranging a route for their surrender.

They said they had recognized that the alliance the defunct TPLF had forged with Shabia under what they described as the “Tsimbedo” approach was harmful to the people of Tigray.

They said Shabia had acted as an enemy of the Ethiopian people while inflicting suffering on the people of Tigray.

The surrendered fighters said they believe the questions of the people of Tigray can be resolved through dialogue and mutual understanding rather than through armed conflict.

The Northwestern Command said the militants brought with them more than 280 individual and group weapons, various types of ammunition, battlefield binoculars and other military documents.

Among those who surrendered are commanders and leaders at different levels, including a division commander as well as battalion and company-level leaders, the command said.

The combatants said they rejected efforts by the illegal TPLF leadership to mobilize young people from Tigray for war in an attempt to protect their own interests and evade accountability.

They said the differences facing the people can be resolved through dialogue rather than according to the wishes of a few leaders of the banned TPLF.

The surrendered militants further said the defunct TPLF has shown no willingness to break away from the cycle of war and is continuing an approach that seeks to plunge the people of Tigray into deeper hardship.

They said the group has rejected peaceful alternatives presented to it and lost acceptance among the people of Tigray.

The fighters also said many young people in Tigray are currently waiting for an opportunity to surrender after rejecting the rule of the illegal TPLF and choosing peace.

They said the banned TPLF has been forcing young people into preparations for war in an attempt to separate the people of Tigray from the rest of the Ethiopian people and deny them peace.

According to the surrendered combatants, young people who were forced into the fighting are increasingly recognizing the situation and are ready to surrender when circumstances allow.

The latest surrender involves nearly 300 militants, including commanders at several levels, and the handover of more than 280 weapons together with ammunition, battlefield equipment and documents to the ENDF Northwestern Command in the Tekeze area.

item.title: AU Commission Warns Red Sea Disruption Could Hit African Economies, Global Trade and Energy Security
item.dc:creator: Mesafint Brlie
item.description: Addis Ababa, September 17, 2026 (FMC) — The African Union Commission has warned that actions obstructing or threatening navigation along the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait could carry serious consequences for African economies, international trade, global supply chains and energy security. The Commission made the warning while expressing deep concern over the recent military […]
item.content:encoded:
Addis Ababa, September 17, 2026 (FMC) — The African Union Commission has warned that actions obstructing or threatening navigation along the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait could carry serious consequences for African economies, international trade, global supply chains and energy security.

The Commission made the warning while expressing deep concern over the recent military escalation in the Red Sea region, including attacks targeting the territory of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and international maritime navigation.

In a statement, the Commission condemned attacks carried out by the Houthis against civilian targets and economic infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, as well as attacks and threats against commercial shipping in the Red Sea.

It expressed particular concern over reports of attempted attacks targeting Makkah and other holy cities in Saudi Arabia, stressing that holy sites, civilians and pilgrims visiting them must be fully protected and must under no circumstances become targets of military action.

The Commission strongly reaffirmed the principle of freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in accordance with international law, emphasizing the strategic importance of the maritime route to the littoral states and the wider international community.

It underscored that the security of the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait is also a major strategic interest for Africa, particularly for the states of the Horn of Africa and other Red Sea littoral states.

The Commission further warned against the risk of a wider regionalization of the ongoing confrontations in the Middle East, saying that their security, humanitarian and economic consequences would directly affect the African continent.

It therefore called for the immediate cessation of attacks against civilians, civilian and economic infrastructure, and commercial shipping, as well as respect for freedom of navigation and urgent de-escalation.

The Commission reiterated the need to prioritize dialogue and political avenues to prevent further expansion of hostilities and preserve peace, security and stability throughout the Red Sea region.

item.title: Ethiopia-China ‘All-Weather Strategic Partnership’ Producing “Rich Results” Across Multiple Fields – Diplomat
item.dc:creator: Mesafint Brlie
item.description: Addis Ababa, September 17, 2026 (FMC) — Ethiopia-China cooperation is expanding across infrastructure, trade, education, healthcare, artificial intelligence and other strategic sectors, reflecting the deepening of the two countries’ all-weather strategic partnership, Chinese Embassy Chargé d’Affaires a.i. Sun Mingxi said. Speaking at a media briefing held at the Chinese Embassy in Addis Ababa on Thursday, […]
item.content:encoded:
Addis Ababa, September 17, 2026 (FMC) — Ethiopia-China cooperation is expanding across infrastructure, trade, education, healthcare, artificial intelligence and other strategic sectors, reflecting the deepening of the two countries’ all-weather strategic partnership, Chinese Embassy Chargé d’Affaires a.i. Sun Mingxi said.

Speaking at a media briefing held at the Chinese Embassy in Addis Ababa on Thursday, Sun highlighted recent developments in bilateral cooperation, including major infrastructure projects, growing trade and logistics links, people-to-people exchanges, medical cooperation and emerging collaboration in artificial intelligence.

He said the all-weather strategic cooperative partnership between Ethiopia and China had continued to deepen in 2026 under the strategic guidance of the two countries’ leaders, producing “rich results” across multiple fields.

The partnership was established in 2023, when the two countries elevated their relations during Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s visit to Beijing. The two sides have continued to describe the partnership as a framework for expanding cooperation in traditional and emerging sectors.

Sun pointed to the recent expansion of the Mojo Dry Port as one of the latest examples of infrastructure cooperation. He said the project, built by China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation, is expected to increase annual cargo-handling capacity from 520,000 TEUs to 1.6 million TEUs and reduce average cargo dwell time from 60 days to eight days.

The expansion was inaugurated by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed last week as part of Ethiopia’s efforts to strengthen its logistics capacity and advance regional trade and economic integration.

Sun also cited the Aysha Wind Power Project in Ethiopia’s Somali Region, which he said began operation in January with an installed capacity of 120 megawatts, describing it as Ethiopia’s largest wind power project to date.

He further highlighted an agreement between Ethiopian Electric Power and Norinco International for the construction of the Assosa 2,400-kV substation, while noting that China has remained Ethiopia’s largest trading partner and a major source of investment.

Trade and logistics cooperation is also gaining momentum, according to Sun, who said China’s zero-tariff treatment for African countries with diplomatic relations with Beijing now includes Ethiopia.

He said the policy is directly benefiting Ethiopian coffee and other products, noting that China has become the fourth-largest export market for Ethiopian coffee.

Sun also cited the Ethiopia Special Session of the “Export to China” program held in Addis Ababa on August 19, where enterprises signed 33 cooperation agreements valued at more than 330 million U.S. dollars.

He said the opening of an Ethiopian Airlines all-cargo service between Chengdu and Addis Ababa on August 28, operating twice a week, would further strengthen trade links between the two countries.

People-to-people cooperation is another expanding dimension of the partnership, Sun said, pointing to a recently signed agreement on Chinese-language education under which China will support Ethiopia over the next five years through curriculum development, teaching experts, textbooks and teacher training.

He also highlighted agricultural training programs involving Ethiopian officials, as well as workshops on dryland agriculture, water-saving irrigation and green and low-carbon development held in China.

Medical cooperation, which dates back decades, remains another important component of Ethiopia-China relations, Sun said.

According to the Chargé d’Affaires, China has sent 27 medical teams to Ethiopia since 1974. He said the 26th medical team treated about 76,000 patient visits, conducted more than 3,200 surgeries and helped 506 cataract patients regain their sight during its tenure.

He also highlighted the launch in Addis Ababa in July of the China-Africa Minimally Invasive Medicine Partnership Program, including the establishment of the China-Africa Surgical Robot Training Center — Ethiopia Center and the China-Africa Endoscopic Technology Training Center — Ethiopia Center.

On emerging areas of cooperation, Sun said Ethiopia’s participation in the newly established World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) could open new opportunities for bilateral collaboration in artificial intelligence, the digital economy and other technology-driven sectors.

Ethiopia signed the agreement establishing WAICO in Shanghai in July as one of its 29 founding member states and one of 10 African founding members, according to Sun.

Beyond bilateral relations, the Chargé d’Affaires briefed journalists on China’s economic development, technological advances, green transition and international cooperation, as well as China’s engagement with Africa and the BRICS cooperation mechanism.

Expounding on Beijing’s trade engagements with African nations, he said China-Africa trade reached 239.581 billion U.S. dollars from January to July 2026, marking a 23.5-percent year-on-year increase, while noting that several African agricultural and food products have gained wider access to the Chinese market.

Sun further highlighted China’s implementation of zero-tariff treatment for the 53 African countries with which it maintains diplomatic relations, saying the measure is intended to expand African exports to the Chinese market.

The briefing was held as part of the 2026 China-Africa Year of People-to-People Exchanges, providing an overview of China’s modernization drive, Ethiopia-China relations and cooperation under BRICS.

Ethiopia and China are both members of BRICS, with the two countries also maintaining extensive cooperation through the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation and other multilateral platforms. Ethiopia joined BRICS in 2024, while bilateral ties have continued to develop alongside cooperation in infrastructure, trade, energy, digital technology and other sectors.

 

By Mesafint Brlie

item.title: IGAD Members Endorse Regional Agrifood Plan, Seed Policy to Advance Food Security and Regional Trade
item.dc:creator: Mesafint Brlie
item.description: Addis Ababa, September 17, 2026 (FMC) — IGAD Member States have endorsed the Regional Agrifood Systems Investment Plan (RASIP) 2026–2035 and the Regional Seed Policy and Regulatory Framework, marking a major step toward coordinated action on food security, resilience and sustainable agrifood systems transformation across the Horn of Africa. The two frameworks were endorsed at […]
item.content:encoded:
Addis Ababa, September 17, 2026 (FMC) — IGAD Member States have endorsed the Regional Agrifood Systems Investment Plan (RASIP) 2026–2035 and the Regional Seed Policy and Regulatory Framework, marking a major step toward coordinated action on food security, resilience and sustainable agrifood systems transformation across the Horn of Africa.

The two frameworks were endorsed at a high-level ministerial session in Addis Ababa today, concluding a three-day process that brought together government officials, technical experts and development partners for final review, validation and endorsement of the regional instruments.

RASIP succeeds the Regional Agricultural Investment Plan (RAIP) 2016–2020 and provides a regional framework for coordinated investment linking agriculture, environment, trade and resilience. The Regional Seed Policy and Regulatory Framework is designed to strengthen seed systems, improve access to quality agricultural inputs and promote cooperation across regional seed value chains.

Speaking at the start of the closing session, IGAD Executive Secretary Dr Workneh Gebeyehu said the endorsement of the two frameworks represents a shift from fragmented initiatives toward unified and systemic regional action.

Workneh said the region is facing mounting pressures from climate shocks, including prolonged droughts, as well as conflicts, economic volatility and population growth, making stronger and more coordinated food systems essential.

He said RASIP provides a mechanism for translating continental commitments into tangible regional action and advances the Comprehensive African Agricultural Development Programme (CAADP) framework by directing investment toward resilient and sustainable food systems.

Workneh also highlighted the plan’s role in advancing regional trade through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), stressing the need for the IGAD region to move beyond emergency food responses and build its capacity to supply continental markets.

He said agrifood transformation also depends on reliable access to high-quality inputs, identifying resilient seeds as a key tool for addressing climate shocks and improving agricultural productivity.

According to Workneh, the Regional Seed Policy Framework will help reduce barriers to regional seed trade by harmonizing regulations across borders, expanding access to climate-smart and high-yielding varieties, and maintaining biosafety, quality assurance and phytosanitary standards.

At the opening of the gathering on September 15, Senait Regassa (PhD), Project Coordinator of IGAD’s Food Systems Resilience Programme (FSRP), said food insecurity driven by climate shocks, conflicts, economic volatility and structural weaknesses in production and market systems requires coordinated investment at scale.

Senait said RASIP brings agriculture, environment, trade and resilience into a coherent regional framework designed to strengthen food security, economic growth and social stability.

She also underscored the importance of the regional seed framework, saying stronger seed systems are essential not only for efficient supply but also for food and seed sovereignty and for ensuring farmers have access to quality varieties adapted to changing climatic conditions and resistant to pests and diseases.

Zena Habtewold, Advisor to Ethiopia’s Minister of Agriculture, said RASIP marks a shift from conventional agricultural production toward a broader and more integrated transformation of agrifood systems.

Zena identified sustainable food production, regional trade and AfCFTA, inclusive financing, nutrition, climate resilience, governance and research among the strategic areas requiring investment.

He highlighted Ethiopia’s experience with irrigated wheat production and improved seed varieties as part of efforts to strengthen domestic agricultural production. He also cited cluster farming, which brings smallholder plots together to facilitate mechanization, improve production quality, expand extension services and strengthen market linkages.

Zena further presented Ethiopia’s Green Legacy Initiative as an example of connecting landscape restoration, agroforestry, soil conservation and fruit-tree development with food and nutrition security.

He called for the implementation arrangements and results framework of RASIP to reflect the realities of IGAD member states and continental priorities, while ensuring that regional investment addresses the needs of smallholder farmers, pastoralists, women and youth.

The Regional Seed Policy and Regulatory Framework was developed through studies, consultations and technical reviews involving IGAD member states and stakeholders. The process included a regional dialogue on seed systems and resilience, a Regional Seed Forum and a virtual consultation in June to review the draft framework and incorporate recommendations.

Both instruments contribute to the implementation of continental commitments under the Kampala Declaration and are flagship interventions under the World Bank-funded Food Systems Resilience Program (FSRP), implemented by IGAD.

Workneh said the endorsement signals the region’s readiness to move beyond policy dialogue toward implementation and financial accountability, pledging IGAD’s institutional support to help member states localize the frameworks and mobilize development partners around their implementation.

He expressed appreciation to member states, development partners and other stakeholders that contributed to the development of the frameworks, as well as the World Bank for supporting the process through the Food Systems Resilience Program for Eastern and Southern Africa.

The endorsement establishes a common regional framework for coordinated investment across food production, agricultural inputs, markets, trade, climate resilience and environmental sustainability, with the broader aim of building a more food-secure, resilient and integrated Horn of Africa.

item.title: Horn of Africa Moves to Turn El Niño Forecast Into Coordinated Early Action
item.dc:creator: Mesafint Brlie
item.description: Addis Ababa, September 17, 2026 (FMC) — IGAD Member States and regional and international partners are moving to translate forecasts of a potentially strong El Niño during the October–December 2026 season into coordinated preparedness, anticipatory financing and early action to protect lives, livelihoods and critical infrastructure across the Horn of Africa. The call came at […]
item.content:encoded:
Addis Ababa, September 17, 2026 (FMC) — IGAD Member States and regional and international partners are moving to translate forecasts of a potentially strong El Niño during the October–December 2026 season into coordinated preparedness, anticipatory financing and early action to protect lives, livelihoods and critical infrastructure across the Horn of Africa.

The call came at the ministerial segment of the IGAD High-Level Ministerial Forum on El Niño Preparedness in the Horn of Africa, held in Addis Ababa as the culmination of a three-day regional process focused on assessing preparedness, identifying priority risks and strengthening cross-border action ahead of the anticipated climate impacts.

Speaking on behalf of the Government of Ethiopia, Deputy Commissioner of the Ethiopia Disaster Risk Management Commission Ayderus Hassan said the potential impact of El Niño 2026 requires technical preparedness to be matched by political leadership, national ownership, regional solidarity, timely financing and early action.

He said Ethiopia is strengthening its disaster management system to become increasingly multi-hazard, impact-based, anticipatory and multi-sectoral, linking monitoring, forecasting, impact assessment, early warning, preparedness, anticipatory action and response.

“For El Niño 2026, this means continuously monitoring risks, identifying potential hotspots, preparing vulnerable communities and sectors, strengthening contingency planning, and taking anticipatory measures before a crisis,” Ayderus said.

He underscored the need for early financing, noting that Ethiopia’s Disaster Risk Response Fund provides a mechanism for predictable financing for disaster risk management, including preparedness, early warning, anticipatory action, response and resilience.

Ayderus also called for stronger regional cooperation through cross-border information sharing, joint risk analysis, interoperable early warning systems and coordinated anticipatory action, as El Niño-related risks could simultaneously affect agriculture, livestock, food security, water, health, infrastructure, livelihoods and population movements.

He said the high-level segment would consider the technical findings, discuss national priorities and endorse the IGAD High-Level Call to Action for El Niño preparedness, with clear responsibilities, resources and mechanisms for monitoring implementation.

IGAD Deputy Executive Secretary Mohamed Abdi Ware said the region’s experience had demonstrated that disasters do not respect national borders and therefore require collective action.

He said IGAD’s climate-centred impact assessment indicates a 90-percent chance of above-normal rainfall over southern Ethiopia, central and southern Somalia and northeastern Kenya, with the closest parallels being the El Niño events of 2023 and 1997.

According to Mohamed, floods in 2023 claimed at least 352 lives across Ethiopia, Kenya and Somalia and displaced more than 2.4 million people. In Somalia, damage and losses in 16 assessed districts exceeded 176 million U.S. dollars, while recovery needs surpassed 210 million dollars.

Recalling his experience as a humanitarian worker during the 1997 El Niño episode, he said the event demonstrated how excessive rainfall could devastate crops and livestock, disrupt livelihoods and contribute to disease outbreaks and economic losses.

“We cannot stop the rain, but we can decide what it finds when it arrives,” Mohamed said, stressing the importance of preparing for foreseeable risks before they materialize.

He said member states are expected to activate their preparedness plans, share warnings across borders, undertake anticipatory measures and monitor and report on actions delivered throughout the season.

Representing Somalia, Minister of Agriculture Mohammed Abdi Hayir stressed the need to draw lessons from the 2023 El Niño experience and ensure that early warning systems lead to rapid and concrete action, supported by adequate financing, operational contingency plans, prepared communities and effective coordination.

The Somali minister also highlighted the interconnected nature of climatic, humanitarian, economic and security risks facing the region.

Representing Djibouti, Executive Secretary for Disaster Risk Management Ahmed Mohamed Mogad said his country is committed to establishing a national multi-hazard early warning system, complemented with IGAD support by a crisis management room connected to five regional branches.

He said flooding, population displacement, food insecurity, health risks, pastoral mobility and trade flows transcend national borders and require a regional response.

Director of the UNDP Resilience Hub for Africa Zeynu Jemal Ummer said weaknesses exposed by recent climate shocks in financing, cross-border coordination, infrastructure and evacuation planning should be viewed as long-term development gaps rather than seasonal shortcomings.

He called for preparedness priorities to be incorporated into national development plans, sector strategies and IGAD frameworks, alongside the integration of disaster-risk financing into national budgets.

Zeynu also urged investment in water storage, transboundary water-transfer systems, watershed restoration, resilient transport corridors and joint management of shared basins to address both flooding and persistent water stress.

IOM Deputy Regional Director for Operations Nihan Erdogan said El Niño should be viewed not only as a climate event but also as a potential mobility and displacement crisis.

She urged countries to “act early, act together, and act for the longer term,” calling for prepositioned supplies, forecast-based financing, evacuation plans, safe sites and protection measures, alongside continuous preparedness and resilient investment.

UNICEF Representative Aboubacar Kampo said more than 162 million children across Eastern and Southern Africa are exposed to the effects of the event, warning that climate shocks could deepen existing food insecurity, displacement, conflict and disease while placing additional pressure on essential services.

He called for forecasts and agreed triggers to unlock financing and action before losses occur, while emphasizing the need to protect climate-resilient water and sanitation, health, nutrition, education, child protection and social protection services.

Kampo also stressed that preparedness must be locally led and adequately resourced, while international and climate-financing institutions should provide timely, flexible and equitable financing for adaptation and anticipatory action.

The three-day forum, held from September 15–17 in Addis Ababa, has brought together ministers, government representatives, technical experts and development and humanitarian partners to assess national and regional preparedness, strengthen cross-border coordination and advance anticipatory financing ahead of the anticipated October–December climate impacts.

The ministerial segment is set to culminate in endorsement of the IGAD Ministerial Call to Action and the Regional Preparedness and Early Action Technical Report, reinforcing the region’s effort to move from forecast to action.
